J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}| $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-5)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-5)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+x-3)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+x-3)=2y\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{aligned}|. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \begin{aligned}J(2,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(2) & 1 \\ 1 & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\ & =4\cdot 2-1\cdot 1 \\ & =7 \\ & \ne 0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3x+2y-1 \\ {x}^{2}+y-4x+4\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=-4-6{x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=-3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-4-6{x}^{2} & 2y \\ 2x & -3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-4-6(0)^{2} & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -3-9(0)^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(-3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-3,\text{ }-4.$ Finally, since we have two real and negative eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy written as $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ where ![](images/60/60be83e58a72728b03ebfa2de6999ec80f17ee29e3f2ab3060d8ca43bbf45de8.svg) and ![](images/98/98bb67f212fa8deee63da1b69ae93086b9eb56a3ec64d70ba36e6a94dff1527b.svg). The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$ \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0. $$ For example, let ![](images/e6/e640b7ca9ddc8252223ec70f011147a702cd25bca0ee8a20314693695c1bec40.svg) First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium. Now, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1+2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have ![](images/93/93058061ca42daa7114b615bcb77a8f9ccbc9cdccec98559db3eb288a7208940.svg) Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/72/72feeca197610c24c70b01f4c1075c75eebe89ae29f1aced83caeb252c275cce.svg) to get $$ \begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222496 :tutorial/content "Suppose the system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ is almost linear at an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ In this case, the system's behavior near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ can be approximated by a linear system. First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by $$ \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast. $$ Small values of $\mathbf{u}$ correspond to points close to the equilibrium. Next, assuming $\mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,$ we compute the Jacobian matrix ![](images/7a/7a0ff677dae0e51e34aed63faadfcb31f277f060c03488fdc1828cf8a2a5a0ec.svg) and evaluate it at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to obtain the constant matrix $J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).$ Finally, since $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ the nonlinear system can be approximated by the **linearized system** $$ \mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}. $$ This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222495 :tutorial/content "Again, suppose $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium of the nonlinear system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ and assume the system is *almost linear* at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$. If $$ J=\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast) $$ denotes the Jacobian matrix evaluated at the equilibrium, then the behavior of solutions near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is determined by the eigenvalues of $J.$ This information can be summarized in the following table. | **Eigenvalues of the Jacobian** | **Behavior** | **Stability** | | --- | --- | --- | | real and both positive | source / unstable node | unstable | | real and both negative | sink / stable node | asymptotically stable | | real and opposite signs | saddle | unstable | | complex with positive real part | spiral source | unstable | | complex with negative real part | spiral sink | asymptotically stable | Let's now consider a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222497 :tutorial/content "In the classification above, we intentionally skipped one case: The eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of the Jacobian at the equilibrium are purely imaginary. In this situation, the corresponding linearized system has a *center* at the origin, meaning that solutions neither grow nor decay, but instead circulate around the equilibrium. For the original nonlinear system, however, this case is *inconclusive*. While the linearized system predicts closed orbits, the nonlinear system *may* exhibit a stable center, an unstable spiral, or other nearby behavior. Therefore, when the Jacobian has purely imaginary eigenvalues, linearization alone is not sufficient to classify the equilibrium. In such cases, further analysis beyond linear approximation is required." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221470 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

:question/math-academy-id "q-335146" :question/problem "$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)-7x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+6y(t)\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-7x \\ {x}^{2}+6y\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-7x)=-7,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-7x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+6y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+6y)=6\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2y \\ 2x & 6\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields #uuid "73b75bfd-1216-5131-9b02-68e4ee57dee1" :question/math-academy-id "q-336683" :question/problem "$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x(t))+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y(t)^{2}+1) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t)+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x(t))\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$ $\,$ The equilibrium is an {{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1) \\ 5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x)\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=5\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} & 5\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) & \frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+(0)^{2}} & 5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & 0 \\ 1 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=3,\text{ }5.$ Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues,, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy #uuid "3df14087-9cbc-58b7-a996-90852883ca3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-336937" :question/problem "$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)-2x(t)^{3}+y(t)^{2} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)-3y(t)^{3}+x(t)^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$ $\,$ The equilibrium is an {{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $$ \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} \\ -3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=-4-6{x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=-3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-4-6{x}^{2} & 2y \\ 2x & -3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-4-6(0)^{2} & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -3-9(0)^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(-3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-3,\text{ }-4.$ Finally, since we have two real and negative eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy written as $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ where ![](images/60/60be83e58a72728b03ebfa2de6999ec80f17ee29e3f2ab3060d8ca43bbf45de8.svg) and ![](images/98/98bb67f212fa8deee63da1b69ae93086b9eb56a3ec64d70ba36e6a94dff1527b.svg). The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$ \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0. $$ For example, let ![](images/e6/e640b7ca9ddc8252223ec70f011147a702cd25bca0ee8a20314693695c1bec40.svg) First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium. Now, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1+2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have ![](images/93/93058061ca42daa7114b615bcb77a8f9ccbc9cdccec98559db3eb288a7208940.svg) Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/72/72feeca197610c24c70b01f4c1075c75eebe89ae29f1aced83caeb252c275cce.svg) to get $$ \begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222496 :tutorial/content "Suppose the system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ is almost linear at an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ In this case, the system's behavior near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ can be approximated by a linear system. First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by $$ \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast. $$ Small values of $\mathbf{u}$ correspond to points close to the equilibrium. Next, assuming $\mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,$ we compute the Jacobian matrix ![](images/7a/7a0ff677dae0e51e34aed63faadfcb31f277f060c03488fdc1828cf8a2a5a0ec.svg) and evaluate it at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to obtain the constant matrix $J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).$ Finally, since $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ the nonlinear system can be approximated by the **linearized system** $$ \mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}. $$ This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222495 :tutorial/content "Again, suppose $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium of the nonlinear system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ and assume the system is *almost linear* at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$. If $$ J=\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast) $$ denotes the Jacobian matrix evaluated at the equilibrium, then the behavior of solutions near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is determined by the eigenvalues of $J.$ This information can be summarized in the following table. | **Eigenvalues of the Jacobian** | **Behavior** | **Stability** | | --- | --- | --- | | real and both positive | source / unstable node | unstable | | real and both negative | sink / stable node | asymptotically stable | | real and opposite signs | saddle | unstable | | complex with positive real part | spiral source | unstable | | complex with negative real part | spiral sink | asymptotically stable | Let's now consider a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222497 :tutorial/content "In the classification above, we intentionally skipped one case: The eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of the Jacobian at the equilibrium are purely imaginary. In this situation, the corresponding linearized system has a *center* at the origin, meaning that solutions neither grow nor decay, but instead circulate around the equilibrium. For the original nonlinear system, however, this case is *inconclusive*. While the linearized system predicts closed orbits, the nonlinear system *may* exhibit a stable center, an unstable spiral, or other nearby behavior. Therefore, when the Jacobian has purely imaginary eigenvalues, linearization alone is not sufficient to classify the equilibrium. In such cases, further analysis beyond linear approximation is required." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221470 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-2x(t)+3y(t)+3 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)+2{y}^{2}(t)-y(t)+5\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }-1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
"] ["question-4189cf97-4019-5e9f-9f66-1a0dc740de8d" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+3y+3 \\ -4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=-4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=4y-1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4y-1\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(2)-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4(-1)-1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]. $$"] ["question-4189cf97-4019-5e9f-9f66-1a0dc740de8d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-7x)=-7,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-7x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+6y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+6y)=6\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2y \\ 2x & 6\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]. $$"] our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y+(x-2)^{3}+8)=3(x-2)^{2} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x(t)+4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y(t)+8))=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+8))=-2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x(t)+4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y(t)+8))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+8)\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}3(x-2)^{2} & 1 \\ -2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(y+8)\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }-8]^{T}$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3((2)-2)^{2} & 1 \\ -2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(-8+8)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]. $$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0-\lambda & 1 \\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}i.$ Since we have two complex eigenvalues with positive real $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}-3x+{y}^{2} \\ -2y+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3x+{y}^{2})=-3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+{x}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+{x}^{2})=-2\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2y \\ 2x & -2\end{aligned}]. $$ Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2,\text{ }-3.$ Finally, since we have two real and negative eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$"] :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+y-1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1)\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-1)=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-1)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1))=\frac{1}{x+3} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-y-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-1))=-1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ \frac{1}{x+3} & -1\end{aligned}]. $$ Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda & 1 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-\frac{1}{3} & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1)-\frac{1}{3} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -\frac{1}{3} & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{6}.$ Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$"] ["question-74a51538-7992-5c00-9322-0a9614a20c67" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1) \\ 5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x)\end{aligned}].$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}] $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=5\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} & 5\end{aligned}]. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) & \frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+(0)^{2}} & 5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & 0 \\ 1 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=3,\text{ }5.$ Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues,, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$"] ["question-73b75bfd-1216-5131-9b02-68e4ee57dee1" at ${x}^{∗}.$" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}2(0) & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$"} {:db/id 17592186368108 :question/id #uuid "4b642f63-61e2-5bfd-b745-caa14baed777" at ${x}^{∗}.$" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-0\cdot 0 \\  & =4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$"} {:db/id 17592186368125 :question/id #uuid "267b0a4d-f99c-548c-bed7-e5ca46d9be25" First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & \pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \pi (0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & 2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+x(t)y(t)-2x(t)+3y(t)+5 \\ {y}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)-x(t)+4y(t)+4\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }-1]^{T}?$

| ${u}^{′}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5 \\ {y}^{2}-x+4y+4\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=2x+y-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=x+3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=2y+4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y-2 & x+3 \\ -1 & 2y+4\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(1)+(-1)-2 & 1+3 \\ -1 & 2(-1)+4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221419 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221183 :question/id #uuid "fd2d2d61-53a6-51c1-811c-41393270ddba" :question/math-academy-id "e-21676"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "777fae40-2377-5e63-89f6-5c857beba2b2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990} {:db/id 17592186048992} {:db/id 17592186049209} {:db/id 17592186050001} {:db/id 17592186050967}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221971 :question/id #uuid "e06a687f-dc13-5f88-9f73-09d6b8609d29" :question/math-academy-id "q-333532"} {:db/id 17592186222008 :question/id #uuid "cf73bc56-7b5d-559b-a60d-877501f659c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-335535"} {:db/id 17592186368193 :question/id #uuid "e17b136f-4a98-5e4e-bc96-b1c2003fa4a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-336946"} {:db/id 17592186368201 :question/id #uuid "9ce4d3c5-f9b2-510f-a42c-6aedb52f013f" :question/math-academy-id "q-337695"} {:db/id 17592186385222 :question/id #uuid "e704e213-b49e-50a4-88fd-486e93de3264" :question/math-academy-id "q-336689"} {:db/id 17592186385241 :question/id #uuid "1956c8a5-a177-5c5c-b051-b1da508f8665" :question/math-academy-id "q-337709"}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying an Isolated Critical Point of a Nonlinear System"} {:db/id 17592186221183 :question/id #uuid "fd2d2d61-53a6-51c1-811c-41393270ddba" :question/math-academy-id "e-21676" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186221419 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "777fae40-2377-5e63-89f6-5c857beba2b2" :knowledge-point/title "Classifying an Isolated Critical Point of a Nonlinear System"}] :question/problem "![](images/45/45f0e29c3f9f2c90418de2d78f15dedef030364d08d0dfd7d59fdafc6b58ae5f.png)

"c94f64e0-3901-584e-8de4-83ca8b66843b" :topic/math-academy-id 6378} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222324 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222494 :tutorial/content "Consider an autonomous system written as $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ where $\mathbf{x}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})=[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}(x,y) \\ {f}_{2}(x,y)\end{aligned}]$.

The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$\det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0.$$

For example, let $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), \qquad \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})= [\begin{aligned}x+y+{y}^{2} \\ x+y\end{aligned}], \qquad \mathbf{x}^\ast=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$$

First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium.

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1+2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned}$$ Thus, we have

$$J = |\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2y \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|.$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast = [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned}$$

Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbbe8bd0-4cef-54d0-9803-a59eee727c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14492 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6570665c-9c0e-5698-9c44-79ef60fe6401" :step/math-academy-id 591480 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222325}} {:db/id 17592186222325 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221417 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221182 :question/id #uuid "0f4ae74c-67d0-5c0e-99db-e834253b3851" :question/math-academy-id "e-21675"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bd9680fc-dfa9-5411-aeca-81659b7dec8a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221969} {:db/id 17592186222005} {:db/id 17592186368108} {:db/id 17592186368125} {:db/id 17592186396527} {:db/id 17592186396556}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Almost Linear Systems"} :step/id #uuid "4ea90440-2d8e-5c27-b532-f6be5d45b3b4" :step/math-academy-id 591481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222326}} {:db/id 17592186222326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222496 :tutorial/content "Suppose the system $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ is almost linear at an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ In this case, the system's behavior near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ can be approximated by a linear system.

First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by $$\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast.$$ Small values of $\mathbf{u}$ correspond to points close to the equilibrium.

Next, assuming $\mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,$ we compute the Jacobian matrix $$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x})= [\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}],$$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to obtain the constant matrix $J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).$

Finally, since $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ the nonlinear system can be approximated by the **linearized system** $$\mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}.$$

This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "9356e91f-f080-5827-a567-781aedac309a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14494 :tutorial/title "Linear Approximations Near Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "c10be260-d12b-595c-b241-523d377180f4" :step/math-academy-id 591484 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222327}} {:db/id 17592186222327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221418 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221181 :question/id #uuid "87b69a53-94f5-51e6-9c3a-e403abbf1fa3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21674"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a9aeac73-8ee3-5fef-a47c-a96e3545d89c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049962} {:db/id 17592186050780}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221965} {:db/id 17592186221966} {:db/id 17592186368134} {:db/id 17592186368143} {:db/id 17592186368152} {:db/id 17592186368175} {:db/id 17592186368184}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "264a8b35-ed46-5392-a8ec-e88ead83801a" :step/math-academy-id 591485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222328}} {:db/id 17592186222328 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222495 :tutorial/content "Again, suppose $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium of the nonlinear system $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ and assume the system is *almost linear* at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$. If $$J=\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)$$ denotes the Jacobian matrix evaluated at the equilibrium, then the behavior of solutions near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is determined by the eigenvalues of $J.$

This information can be summarized in the following table.

| **Eigenvalues of the Jacobian** | **Behavior** | **Stability** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| real and both positive | source / unstable node | unstable |
| real and both negative | sink / stable node | asymptotically stable |
| real and opposite signs | saddle | unstable |
| complex with positive real part | spiral source | unstable |
| complex with negative real part | spiral sink | asymptotically stable |

In such cases, further analysis beyond linear approximation is required." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d168b25-7771-5e55-8be8-2eb16080b9b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14496 :tutorial/title "A Note About Stable Centers"} :step/id #uuid "d039d8e2-81e7-5160-bcfd-7765a694f63a" :step/math-academy-id 591492}] :activity/title "Linear Approximations Near Equilibria" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221470} {:db/id 17592186222324 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222494 :tutorial/content "Consider an autonomous system written as $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ where $\mathbf{x}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})=[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}(x,y) \\ {f}_{2}(x,y)\end{aligned}]$.

The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$\det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0.$$

For example, let $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), \qquad \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})= [\begin{aligned}x+y+{y}^{2} \\ x+y\end{aligned}], \qquad \mathbf{x}^\ast=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$$

First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium.

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1+2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned}$$ Thus, we have

$$J = |\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2y \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|.$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast = [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned}$$

Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbbe8bd0-4cef-54d0-9803-a59eee727c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14492 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6570665c-9c0e-5698-9c44-79ef60fe6401" :step/math-academy-id 591480 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222325}} {:db/id 17592186222494 :tutorial/content "Consider an autonomous system written as $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ where $\mathbf{x}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})=[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}(x,y) \\ {f}_{2}(x,y)\end{aligned}]$.

Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbbe8bd0-4cef-54d0-9803-a59eee727c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14492 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222325 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221417 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221182 :question/id #uuid "0f4ae74c-67d0-5c0e-99db-e834253b3851" :question/math-academy-id "e-21675"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bd9680fc-dfa9-5411-aeca-81659b7dec8a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221969} {:db/id 17592186222005} {:db/id 17592186368108} {:db/id 17592186368125} {:db/id 17592186396527} {:db/id 17592186396556}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Almost Linear Systems"} :step/id #uuid "4ea90440-2d8e-5c27-b532-f6be5d45b3b4" :step/math-academy-id 591481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222326}} {:db/id 17592186222326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222496 :tutorial/content "Suppose the system $$\mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),$$ is almost linear at an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ In this case, the system's behavior near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ can be approximated by a linear system.

First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by $$\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast.$$ Small values of $\mathbf{u}$ correspond to points close to the equilibrium.

Next, assuming $\mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,$ we compute the Jacobian matrix $$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x})= [\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}],$$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to obtain the constant matrix $J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).$

Finally, since $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ the nonlinear system can be approximated by the **linearized system** $$\mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}.$$

This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium.

[17592186046660 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid
